etymology: From Old French tache, a fastening or clasp; rendering Hebrew qeres, the hooks or clasps of gold and brass that coupled the tabernacle curtains into one.
biblical_def: Taches are the clasps by which the curtains of the tabernacle were coupled together — fifty of gold for the inner curtains of fine linen, and fifty of brass for the tent of goats’ hair above. The LORD’s own word gives their purpose: “thou shalt make fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle” (Exo 26:6). Ten separate breadths of embroidered work, wrought by many hands, were made ONE dwelling by these small fastenings; without the taches there were curtains, but no tabernacle. The gold clasps stood at the join of the two great sets of curtains, directly over the place of the veil, so that the line of union ran above the way into the holiest. Small things carried the unity of the whole house of God. Let the believer read the lesson the apostle draws for the true tabernacle, the Church: the body is “fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth” (Eph 4:16). The saints are many breadths of diverse weaving, but Christ couples them into one dwelling of God through the Spirit; and the humble members that bind brother to brother are as the taches of gold — little seen, yet bearing the oneness of the whole.
webster_summary: The gold and brass clasps that coupled the tabernacle curtains, making many breadths one dwelling.
webster_full: TACHES, the clasps or fastenings by which the curtains of the tabernacle were coupled.
Fifty of gold joined the inner curtains of fine twined linen; fifty of brass the tent of goats’ hair.
By them the many breadths became one tabernacle, as the LORD commanded.
They stood at the great join of the curtains, over against the veil.
They figure the hidden bonds by which Christ makes His many people one house of God.
scriptures: Exo 26:6
And thou shalt make fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle.
And thou shalt make fifty taches of brass, and put the taches into the loops, and couple the tent together, that it may be one.
And they brought the tabernacle unto Moses, the tent, and all his furniture, his taches, his boards, his bars, and his pillars, and his sockets,
Eph 4:16

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.
corruption_summary: A fastening of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the weight of small, hidden things that carry the unity of the house of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Taches face no postmodern redefinition. The truth they carry rebukes the love of the conspicuous: the age honours the embroidered breadths — the visible, the platformed, the admired — and despises the small clasps that no visitor ever praised, though without them there was no tabernacle at all.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of the hidden bond. God specified the taches as exactly as the cherubim, for the unity of His house hung upon them. So in the Church, the unnoticed members who couple brother to brother — the peacemakers, the intercessors, the faithful joints of supply — bear a weight of glory out of all proportion to their size.
roots_summary: From the Old French for a clasp, taches render the Hebrew qeres, the fifty gold and fifty brass fastenings that made the tabernacle one.
roots_lines: Taches — Old French tache, a fastening; Hebrew qeres.

They stood at the great join, over against the veil.
They figure the hidden bonds that make Christ’s people one house.
usage: Without the taches there were curtains, but no tabernacle.
Small things carried the unity of the whole house of God.
The unnoticed members who couple brother to brother are the taches of gold in Christ’s Church.

etymology: Middle English ouche, a brooch or jewelled setting (from Old French nouche); rendering Hebrew mishbetsōth, the wrought settings of gold in which the stones of the high priest’s ephod were fixed.
biblical_def: Ouches are the settings of gold — sockets of wreathen, embroidered work — that held the precious stones upon the high priest’s shoulders. Upon two onyx stones were graven the names of the children of Israel, six on the one and six on the other, “with the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet”; and the LORD commanded, “thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold” (Exo 28:11). So set, the stones were fastened on the shoulders of the ephod, “for stones of memorial unto the children of Israel: and Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial” (Exo 28:12). The ouches also received the wreathen chains that bound on the breastplate (Exo 28:25). Mark what the ouches did: they held the names of the people fast to the priest, so that Israel could not slip from his shoulders while he stood before God. Here is the believer’s security in his great High Priest. The names of Christ’s people are not laid loosely upon Him but set in Him as stones in gold — graven like a signet, fixed in a setting that cannot fail. He bears His own upon the shoulders of His strength before the face of God, and none shall pluck them thence.
webster_summary: The gold settings that held the engraved memorial stones upon the high priest’s shoulders; the fastness of the saints’ names upon their Priest.
webster_full: OUCHES, sockets or settings of wrought gold, in which precious stones were fixed.
The two onyx stones graven with Israel’s names were set in ouches of gold upon the ephod.
The wreathen chains of the breastplate were also fastened in the ouches.
By them Aaron bore the names of the children of Israel before the LORD for a memorial.
They figure the fastness of the saints’ names, set like signet-graven stones in Christ.
scriptures: With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, shalt thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel: thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold.

And thou shalt put the two stones upon the shoulders of the ephod for stones of memorial unto the children of Israel: and Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial.
And the other two ends of the two wreathen chains thou shalt fasten in the two ouches, and put them on the shoulderpieces of the ephod before it.
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
corruption_summary: A setting of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the fastness of the believer’s name upon his High Priest — set in gold, not laid on loosely.
corruption_paragraphs: Ouches face no postmodern redefinition. The truth they carry answers the trembling saint who fears he may yet slip from the memory or the mercy of God — as though his name were laid loosely upon Christ and might fall in a rough hour.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the security of the saints in their Priest. The names were graven like a signet — cut in, not written on — and then set in ouches of gold so the stones could not drop. So Christ bears His people: engraved and set, carried on the shoulders of His strength before the face of God, and none shall pluck them out of His hand.
roots_summary: From the Middle English for a jewelled setting, ouches render the gold sockets that fixed Israel’s engraved memorial stones on the high priest’s ephod.

Israel could not slip from the priest’s shoulders while he stood before God.
He bears His own upon the shoulders of His strength, and none shall pluck them thence.

etymology: From Old French chapitel, Latin capitellum, “little head”; the capital or crowning head of a pillar, as in the tabernacle court and the brazen pillars of Solomon’s temple.
biblical_def: A chapiter is the head or capital that crowns a pillar. The pillars of the tabernacle court had their chapiters overlaid with silver (Exo 38:17), and those of the door with gold (Exo 36:38); but the most famous are the two chapiters of the temple porch: “he made two chapiters of molten brass, to set upon the tops of the pillars: the height of the one chapiter was five cubits, and the height of the other chapiter was five cubits” (1Ki 7:16) — crowning Jachin and Boaz, wreathed with nets of checker work, chains, and two hundred pomegranates in rows, with lily work upon the top. A pillar is strength; a chapiter is strength crowned with beauty and fruit. The LORD would not have His house held up by bare posts: what stood, stood adorned. And when Judah fell, the sad inventory of the plunder lingers over the chapiters carried to Babylon (2Ki 25:17; Jer 52:22) — glory catalogued in the hour of its loss. Let the believer learn that in God’s house strength and loveliness belong together: “strength and beauty are in his sanctuary” (Psa 96:6). The pillar that bears must also bloom; the man made strong to uphold others is crowned, in God’s design, with lily work and pomegranates — gentleness and fruitfulness atop the strength.
webster_summary: The capital crowning a pillar; in the sanctuary, strength crowned with lily work and pomegranates — beauty and fruit atop the load-bearing.
webster_full: CHAPITER, the upper part or capital of a pillar or column.
The court pillars’ chapiters were overlaid with silver, the door pillars’ with gold.
Two chapiters of molten brass, five cubits high, crowned Jachin and Boaz at the temple porch.
They were wreathed with checker nets, chains, pomegranates, and lily work.
They witness that in God’s house strength is crowned with beauty and fruit.
scriptures: And he made two chapiters of molten brass, to set upon the tops of the pillars: the height of the one chapiter was five cubits, and the height of the other chapiter was five cubits:

And the sockets for the pillars were of brass; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets of silver; and the overlaying of their chapiters of silver; and all the pillars of the court were filleted with silver.

The height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits, and the chapiter upon it was brass: and the height of the chapiter three cubits; and the wreathen work, and pomegranates upon the chapiter round about, all of brass: and like unto these had the second pillar with wreathen work.
Psa 96:6
Honour and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.
corruption_summary: An ornament of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the union of strength and beauty — the pillar that bears must also bloom.
corruption_paragraphs: Chapiter faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it carries corrects two opposite errors about strength: the brutalist error, which prizes bare load-bearing force and scorns adornment as weakness; and the decorative error, which loves lily work that holds nothing up.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is strength crowned. God set five cubits of wreathen beauty on top of every load-bearing pillar of His porch; He joins in one design what men split apart. The man called to be a pillar in the house of God is to be crowned with gentleness and fruit — pomegranates and lilies atop the brass — for strength and beauty are in His sanctuary.
roots_summary: From the Latin for “little head,” a chapiter is the capital crowning a pillar — in God’s house, strength topped with lily work and fruit.
roots_lines: Chapiter — Old French chapitel, Latin capitellum, little head.
The tabernacle court chapiters were silver; the door pillars’ gold.
Two brass chapiters, five cubits high, crowned Jachin and Boaz.
They bore checker nets, chains, pomegranates, and lily work.
The plunder lists linger over them in the fall of Jerusalem (2Ki 25:17).
usage: A pillar is strength; a chapiter is strength crowned with beauty and fruit.
God would not have His house held up by bare posts: what stood, stood adorned.
The man made a pillar in God’s house is crowned with gentleness and fruitfulness.

etymology: From Old French filet, a little thread or band; rendering Hebrew chāshūqīm, the silver connecting-rods or bands that joined the pillars of the tabernacle court.
biblical_def: Fillets are the silver rods or bands that ran from pillar to pillar around the court of the tabernacle, joining the whole enclosure into one: “the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver” (Exo 27:10), and again in the record of the work, “all the pillars of the court were filleted with silver” (Exo 38:17). Each pillar stood in its socket of brass, but no pillar stood to itself: the fillets tied post to post, bearing the hangings of fine twined linen that walled the holy court from the camp. The silver of these bands was the atonement money, the half-shekel ransom of the numbered people (Exo 38:25-28) — so that the very metal binding the pillars together was redemption silver. There is the picture entire: pillars joined to one another by ransom, and only so enclosing a holy place. Let the believer read it plainly. What binds the saints into one visible fellowship, pillar to pillar around God’s court, is not affinity or interest but the common ransom — “ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold… but with the precious blood of Christ” (1Pe 1:18-19). Churches are not held in line by hoops of steel but by bands of redemption; loose a man from the ransom and he swings out of the fence of the sanctuary.
webster_summary: The silver bands joining the court pillars pillar to pillar — forged from the atonement money; redemption is what ties the saints in line.
webster_full: FILLETS, the connecting rods or bands, overlaid with silver, that joined the pillars of the tabernacle court.
The hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver; the sockets of brass.
They bore the hangings of fine twined linen that enclosed the holy court.
Their silver was the atonement money, the half-shekel ransom of the numbered people.
They figure the common redemption that binds the saints into one visible fellowship.
scriptures: And the twenty pillars thereof and their twenty sockets shall be of brass; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver.

And the sockets for the pillars were of brass; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets of silver; and the overlaying of their chapiters of silver; and all the pillars of the court were filleted with silver.
And the silver of them that were numbered of the congregation was an hundred talents, and a thousand seven hundred and threescore and fifteen shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary:
Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;
corruption_summary: A band of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the truth that redemption, not affinity, is what joins the pillars of God’s court.
corruption_paragraphs: Fillets face no postmodern redefinition. The truth they carry answers the modern recipe for fellowship — affinity groups, shared demographics, common interests — bands of anything but ransom, which hold only while the affinity lasts.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church is bound with redemption silver. The bands joining pillar to pillar were forged from the atonement money of the numbered people; what ties saint to saint is the common price paid, the precious blood of Christ. Fellowship built on less will part at the first strain; the fillets of ransom hold the court in line.
roots_summary: From the Old French for a little band, fillets render the silver rods — forged of atonement money — that joined the court pillars into one enclosure.
roots_lines: Fillets — Old French filet, a band; Hebrew chāshūqīm.
Silver rods joining the tabernacle-court pillars pillar to pillar.
They bore the linen hangings that walled the holy court.
Their silver was the half-shekel atonement money of the numbered people.
They figure the common ransom binding the saints in one fellowship.
usage: No pillar stood to itself: the fillets tied post to post around God’s court.
The metal binding the pillars was redemption silver — the ransom of the numbered.
Churches are not held in line by hoops of steel but by bands of redemption.

etymology: From Middle English knop, a knob or bud; rendering Hebrew kaphtor (the almond-bud swellings of the golden candlestick) and peqa‘im (the gourd-shaped carvings of the temple walls and the molten sea).
biblical_def: Knops are the bud-shaped swellings wrought into the sacred things. On the golden candlestick every branch bore its cups “made like unto almonds, with a knop and a flower” — “his shaft, and his branches, his bowls, his knops, and his flowers, shall be of the same” (Exo 25:31), all beaten of one talent of pure gold. In Solomon’s temple the cedar lining was “carved with knops and open flowers” (1Ki 6:18), and under the brim of the molten sea ran two rows of knops, “cast in two rows, when it was cast” (1Ki 7:24). The knop is the bud — life swelling but not yet open — set everywhere between stem and flower, promise between root and bloom. The candlestick that gave light in the holy place was formed as a living almond tree in gold: knop, flower, and fruit-cup on every branch, the tree of watching (for the almond is the wakeful tree, Jer 1:11-12) blossoming in the lamplight. Let the believer take the quiet doctrine of the bud: God’s workmanship carries life in stages, and He carves even the not-yet-open into His house. Grace in the bud is grace indeed; the knop belongs to the candlestick as surely as the flower. He who begins the swelling will bring on the bloom, being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work will perform it (Php 1:6).
webster_summary: The bud-shaped swellings of the golden candlestick and temple carvings; grace in the bud, carved into God’s house as surely as the open flower.
webster_full: KNOPS, knobs or buds; ornamental swellings wrought into the sacred furniture and walls.
Every branch of the golden candlestick bore its knop and flower, beaten of one talent of gold.
The temple’s cedar lining was carved with knops and open flowers.
Two rows of knops ran under the brim of the molten sea, cast when it was cast.
They figure life in the bud — the not-yet-open carved into God’s house with the bloom.
scriptures: And thou shalt make a candlestick of pure gold: of beaten work shall the candlestick be made: his shaft, and his branches, his bowls, his knops, and his flowers, shall be of the same.
And the cedar of the house within was carved with knops and open flowers: all was cedar; there was no stone seen.
And under the brim of it round about there were knops compassing it, ten in a cubit, compassing the sea round about: the knops were cast in two rows, when it was cast.
Php 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: An ornament of the sanctuary, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the standing of grace in the bud — the beginner belongs to the candlestick as truly as the bloom.
corruption_paragraphs: Knops face no postmodern redefinition. The truth they carry answers the impatience that despises small beginnings — the church culture that celebrates only the open flower and the finished fruit, and has no place for the swelling bud.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of the not-yet-open. God commanded the knop wrought into the candlestick beside the flower, of the same beaten gold; He carves stages of life into His house. The young believer, the tender conscience, the grace just swelling — these belong to the light-bearing tree as surely as the mature bloom, and He who began the work will bring on the flower.
roots_summary: From the Middle English for a bud or knob, knops name the almond-bud swellings of the candlestick and the carved buds of the temple and molten sea.
roots_lines: Knops — Middle English knop, a knob or bud; Hebrew kaphtor / peqa‘im.
Every candlestick branch bore its knop and flower, of one beaten talent.
The temple cedar was carved with knops and open flowers.
Two cast rows of knops compassed the molten sea.
The knop is the bud — promise set between root and bloom.
usage: Grace in the bud is grace indeed; the knop belongs to the candlestick as surely as the flower.
God carves even the not-yet-open into His house.
He who begins the swelling will bring on the bloom (Php 1:6).

etymology: From Old French haubergeon, diminutive of hauberc, a coat of mail; in the King James Version, a corslet or mail-coat, and the figure for the woven collar of the high priest’s robe.
biblical_def: A habergeon is a coat of mail, the armored shirt of the soldier. The word does double duty in the Scriptures. In the armories it is plain war-gear: Uzziah prepared for his host “shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons” (2Ch 26:14), and Nehemiah’s builders wrought with weapons at hand while “the rulers were behind all the house of Judah” and half the servants held “the spears, the shields, and the bows, and the habergeons” (Neh 4:16). But its most striking use is in the sanctuary: the robe of the ephod was woven with a collar “as it were the hole of an habergeon, that it be not rent” (Exo 28:32) — the priest’s garment bound like armor at the throat so it could not tear. Job’s LORD even asks whether leviathan can be taken by one who dares come at him “with a habergeon” (Job 41:26, the “coat of mail” there). So the mail-coat guards the vitals of the fighting man, and the priest’s robe borrows its strength at the point of strain. Let the believer see both offices joined in Christ and in His people: the servant of God is at once priest and soldier — robed for worship, armored for war — and the garment of his calling is woven not to rend. Put on the whole armour of God; and what God has woven of your office, let no man tear.
webster_summary: A coat of mail; the armored shirt of the soldier, and the figure for the untearable collar of the high priest’s robe.
webster_full: HABERGEON, a coat of mail; a corslet defending the neck and breast.
Uzziah armed his host with shields, spears, helmets, and habergeons.
Nehemiah’s builders laboured while half held spears, shields, bows, and habergeons.
The robe of the ephod had its collar woven “as it were the hole of an habergeon, that it be not rent.”
It joins the two offices: robed for worship, armored for war.
scriptures: And there shall be an hole in the top of it, in the midst thereof: it shall have a binding of woven work round about the hole of it, as it were the hole of an habergeon, that it be not rent.
And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones.
Neh 4:16

And it came to pass from that time forth, that the half of my servants wrought in the work, and the other half of them held both the spears, the shields, and the bows, and the habergeons; and the rulers were behind all the house of Judah.
Eph 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
corruption_summary: A piece of armor and a priestly figure, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the double office of the man of God — robed for worship, armored for war.
corruption_paragraphs: Habergeon faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it carries answers the age’s split religion: a worship stripped of warfare, all robe and no mail; or a combativeness stripped of worship, all mail and no robe — both tearing what God wove together.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the joined office. The priest’s robe was bound at the throat like a soldier’s mail, that it be not rent; Nehemiah’s men built with the trowel and stood by the habergeon in the same hour. The servant of Christ worships as a soldier and wars as a worshipper, and the garment of his calling is woven not to tear.
roots_summary: From the Old French for a little mail-coat, habergeon names the soldier’s corslet and the untearable collar of the priest’s robe.
roots_lines: Habergeon — Old French haubergeon, diminutive of hauberc, mail-coat.
Uzziah’s armories and Nehemiah’s wall-builders carried habergeons.
The robe of the ephod was collared “as it were the hole of an habergeon.”
The mail guards the vitals; the robe borrows its strength at the strain-point.
It figures the joined office: priest and soldier in one man.
usage: The priest’s robe was bound like armor at the throat, that it be not rent.

etymology: From Latin cornu, a horn; in the King James Version rendering the Hebrew shophar-kin and the Aramaic qarna of Daniel — a curved horn blown in worship, in triumph, and, at Babylon, in coerced idolatry.
biblical_def: The cornet is a horn for blowing — and the Scriptures show it serving two masters. Before the ark, “David and all the house of Israel played before the LORD on all manner of instruments made of fir wood, even on harps, and on psalteries, and on timbrels, and on cornets, and on cymbals” (2Sa 6:5); and the psalm commands, “With trumpets and sound of cornet make a joyful noise before the LORD, the King” (Psa 98:6). But in Babylon the same voice of the horn opens the tyrant’s liturgy: “at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image” (Dan 3:5). The instrument is the same; the worship it summons is not. A horn has no doctrine: it lends its voice to whatever throne commands it, calling Israel to the ark or the provinces to the image. Therefore the question is never merely what is played, but who is obeyed when it sounds. Three men in Babylon heard the cornet with everyone else and did not bow; the summons reached their ears but not their knees. Let the believer keep that distinction: the world’s music will sound on schedule, and the crowd will fall on cue — but the sound of a horn is not the voice of God.
webster_summary: A horn for blowing — sounding before the ark in true worship and at Babylon summoning the crowd to the golden image; the same instrument, two masters.
webster_full: CORNET, a wind instrument; a curved horn blown with the breath.
David and all Israel played on cornets before the ark of the LORD.
The psalm commands the cornet’s joyful noise before the LORD, the King.
At Babylon the cornet opened Nebuchadnezzar’s summons to worship the image.
It witnesses that instruments serve whatever worship commands them.
scriptures: Psa 98:6
With trumpets and sound of cornet make a joyful noise before the LORD, the King.
And David and all the house of Israel played before the LORD on all manner of instruments made of fir wood, even on harps, and on psalteries, and on timbrels, and on cornets, and on cymbals.
Dan 3:5

That at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up:
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
corruption_summary: The cornet exposes the oldest trick of coerced conformity: culture sounds its music on schedule and expects every knee on cue — but a horn is not the voice of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Here the corruption is ancient and present at once. Babylon’s genius was liturgical: not an argument for the image but an orchestra for it — when the music sounds, everyone bows, and the falling crowd itself becomes the sermon. The age works the same way still; its anthems play on schedule, the cameras find the kneeling, and refusal is read not as conviction but as defiance of the whole assembled world.

The answer of the three is the recovered principle: they heard everything and bowed to nothing. “Be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18) — spoken while the furnace roared. The believer trains his knees to a different summons; the cornet of the LORD will sound at the last (1Th 4:16), and it is that trumpet, not Babylon’s, for which he keeps his worship.
roots_summary: From the Latin for horn, cornet names the blown horn that praised the LORD before the ark and summoned Babylon to the image — one instrument, two masters.
roots_lines: Cornet — Latin cornu, a horn; Aramaic qarna in Daniel.
David and all Israel played on cornets before the ark.
“With trumpets and sound of cornet” the psalm commands joyful noise.
At Babylon the cornet opened the summons to the golden image.
Three men heard it with everyone else and did not bow.
usage: A horn has no doctrine: it lends its voice to whatever throne commands it.
The world’s music will sound on schedule, and the crowd will fall on cue.
The summons reached their ears but not their knees (Dan 3).

etymology: From Old French saqueboute; in the King James Version rendering the Aramaic sabbeka of Daniel 3 — properly a triangular stringed instrument (the Greek sambuca), named among Babylon’s orchestra of coerced worship.
biblical_def: The sackbut appears only in the third chapter of Daniel, always in the roll-call of Nebuchadnezzar’s orchestra: “the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick” (Dan 3:5, 7, 10, 15). The English translators borrowed the name of a slide-trumpet of their own day, but the Aramaic sabbeka was a small triangular harp of piercing tone — either way, one more voice in the ensemble that played the provinces to their knees. Mark how the Spirit tells the story: four times the instrument list is repeated, nearly word for word, until the reader is as weary of it as the plain of Dura must have been. That repetition is the point. Idolatry of this kind works by saturation — the same sounds, the same summons, over and over, until bowing becomes reflex and the knee no longer consults the conscience. Against the four-fold orchestra stand three men who had heard it all and answered once: “we are not careful to answer thee in this matter” (Dan 3:16). Let the believer learn what the sackbut teaches by its very tedium: the world’s liturgies win by repetition, not by argument; and the guard against them is a conscience that does not grow deaf to God however often Babylon plays the same tune.
webster_summary: One voice in Nebuchadnezzar’s four-times-repeated orchestra of coerced worship; the world’s liturgies win by repetition, not argument.

corruption_summary: Babylon’s orchestra shows conformity manufactured by saturation — the same summons repeated until bowing becomes reflex; the sackbut names the method.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is a method, and it has never retired. Nebuchadnezzar did not argue for his image; he scored it. The same list of instruments, the same command, four times over — saturation in place of persuasion, until all the people, the nations, and the languages fell down on cue. The present age runs the same score through its screens: repeat the anthem often enough and dissent begins to feel not wrong but impossible.

The recovered principle is the unconformed mind. “Be not conformed to this world” (Rom 12:2) is spoken to people inside the orchestra’s range, who will hear Babylon’s music daily. The three did not silence the sackbut; they outlasted it, with a conscience that stayed tuned to God however often the tune returned. Repetition can bend a reflex; it cannot bend a renewed mind.
roots_summary: Rendering the Aramaic sabbeka, the sackbut sounds only in Daniel 3’s four-fold orchestra — the score of coerced conformity, outlasted by three unconformed men.

etymology: From Old French doulcemer, “sweet melody” (Latin dulce melos); in the King James Version rendering the Aramaic sumponyah of Daniel 3, most received as a bagpipe or full-consort sound — the sweetness in Babylon’s orchestra.
biblical_def: The dulcimer closes Nebuchadnezzar’s instrument list: “cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick” (Dan 3:5, 10, 15). The Aramaic sumponyah — kin to our word symphony — suggests the full, sweet, blended sound: whether a bagpipe’s sustained drone or the consort of the whole ensemble sounding together. Its English name confesses the same: dulce melos, sweet melody. And that is precisely its office in the chapter — the sweetness of the summons. Babylon did not drive the nations to the image with whips at the first; it drew them with loveliness, the golden statue gleaming and the symphony swelling, so that bowing felt less like submission than like being carried by something beautiful. The furnace stood behind the music (Dan 3:6), but the music went first. Herein is the abiding warning: sweetness is not sanction. A thing may be genuinely lovely — the melody really was melodious — and summon the soul to an abomination. The three young men were proof against the drone as well as the threat; beauty did not bend what the furnace could not burn. Let the believer test every sweet sound by the throne it serves, for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light (2Co 11:14), and his liturgies are seldom ugly.
webster_summary: The “sweet melody” closing Babylon’s orchestra — loveliness recruited to summon worship of the image; sweetness is not sanction.

corruption_summary: The dulcimer names the sweetness of the summons: Babylon draws with loveliness before it drives with the furnace — and sweetness is not sanction.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption the dulcimer exposes is seduction by beauty. Babylon led with its loveliest sound: the symphony swelled, the gold gleamed, and bowing felt like being carried by something beautiful rather than commanded by something wicked. The present age perfects the method — its abominations arrive scored, styled, and sweet, so that resistance is made to feel like hatred of beauty itself.

The recovered principle: test the sweetness by the throne it serves. The melody in Dura really was melodious, and it summoned worship of an image with a furnace behind it. Satan comes as an angel of light, and his liturgies are seldom ugly. The three were proof against the drone as well as the threat — beauty did not bend what the furnace could not burn — and their God was blessed by the very king whose music failed (Dan 3:28).

etymology: From Old English besma, a broom of bound twigs; rendering Hebrew mat’at’ē, the sweeping-broom of the LORD’s judgment upon Babylon.
biblical_def: A besom is a broom of bound twigs, the homeliest tool in the house — and the LORD of hosts takes it up exactly once in Scripture, against the proudest city on earth: “I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts” (Isa 14:23). The sentence falls in the great taunt against the king of Babylon, who had said, “I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God” (Isa 14:13). Heaven’s answer to the loftiest boast is the lowliest implement: not a sword for a duel between equals, but a broom for rubbish. Babylon, terror of the nations, is dust on God’s floor; the empire is not battled but swept, and the bittern nests where the throne stood. There is deliberate scorn in the choice, and deliberate comfort too. Scorn, for pride that scales heaven ends as sweepings; comfort, for the saints need not reckon any tyranny grander than God’s housekeeping. Let the believer hold both edges of the besom. Nothing swaggering in this world is too great to be swept — and nothing in the believer’s own heart that exalts itself against God deserves a nobler end. Sin is not to be fenced with; it is to be swept out, as He sweeps.
webster_summary: A broom of bound twigs; the LORD’s chosen implement against Babylon — pride that scales heaven ends as sweepings on God’s floor.

corruption_summary: A broom of judgment, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the scorn of God for pride — the empire that scaled heaven ends as sweepings.
corruption_paragraphs: Besom faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it carries deflates the enduring superstition that evil at scale is majestic — that empires, regimes, and cultural juggernauts must be met on their own grand terms and might, at that size, be beyond removal.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the scorn and the comfort of the broom. Heaven answered the loftiest boast in Scripture with housekeeping: Babylon swept, the bittern nesting where the throne stood. The saints need not tremble before swaggering powers, and the saint must not coddle swaggering sins — what exalts itself against God is not fenced with but swept out.
